The Crown and the Republic: A Case for American Monarchy

An Essay in Favor of Constitutional Monarchy for the United States

Introduction

In 1776, the American colonies rejected not merely a particular king, but the very concept of monarchy itself. Nearly 250 years later, it is worth asking whether that wholesale rejection has served the republic well—or whether, in discarding the crown, the Founders inadvertently planted seeds of instability that now threaten to tear the nation apart. The proposition may seem radical, even absurd, to modern American ears: that the United States should establish a constitutional hereditary monarchy, with a king or queen serving as permanent, non-partisan head of state. Yet when examined through the lens of political stability, national unity, and the lessons of comparative democracy, this proposal emerges not as a retreat into the past, but as a sophisticated solution to distinctly modern problems. America needs a monarch—not to rule, but to reign, and in reigning, to heal.

The Crisis of the Elected Head of State

The American presidency was designed as an experiment: could a republic entrust executive power to an elected citizen who would temporarily hold office and then peacefully surrender it? For much of American history, this experiment succeeded reasonably well. But the 21st century has exposed fundamental weaknesses in the model that the Founders could not have anticipated.

The modern American president serves simultaneously as head of state and head of government—two roles that most successful democracies deliberately separate. As head of government, the president must be partisan; he or she advances a particular agenda, rewards political allies, and necessarily works against political opponents. As head of state, however, the president is expected to represent all Americans, to embody national unity, and to serve as a symbol transcending faction. These roles are fundamentally incompatible.

When President Biden speaks at a national ceremony, roughly half the country sees not the symbol of their nation but the leader of a party they oppose. When President Trump stood before the nation, the same dynamic applied in reverse. Every presidential action—attending a funeral, hosting a state dinner, addressing a national tragedy—is filtered through partisan perception. The office meant to unify has become the focal point of division.

Consider the contrast with constitutional monarchies. When Queen Elizabeth II addressed the British people during the COVID-19 pandemic, she spoke as an unimpeachable symbol of national continuity. Her words carried weight precisely because she had no political agenda, no election to win, no party to serve. She belonged equally to Labour voters and Conservative voters, to Remainers and Brexiteers. No American president can claim such universal legitimacy, and the structure of the office ensures none ever will.

Stability and the Long View

Hereditary monarchy provides something no elected system can: genuine long-term thinking institutionalized at the highest level of government. An elected president, even in the best case, thinks in four-year cycles. Their planning horizon extends to the next election; their incentive structure rewards short-term gains over long-term stewardship.

A monarch, by contrast, is trained from birth to think in generational terms. The crown prince or princess knows they will likely reign for decades and will pass the throne to their children. They have no incentive to mortgage the future for present popularity. Their personal legacy is inseparable from the nation's long-term flourishing.

This is not mere theory. Studies of economic performance consistently show that constitutional monarchies outperform republics on numerous metrics. The ten most stable and prosperous democracies in the world include Norway, Sweden, Denmark, the Netherlands, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, and the United Kingdom—all constitutional monarchies. This is not coincidence. The presence of a permanent, stabilizing head of state who embodies institutional continuity creates an environment conducive to both democratic governance and long-term prosperity.

The monarchical principle also provides insurance against democratic backsliding. In constitutional monarchies, the sovereign serves as a guardian of constitutional norms—a final check against authoritarian overreach. When elected leaders attempt to subvert democratic processes, the monarch can serve as a rallying point for constitutional legitimacy. Spain's King Juan Carlos I famously defended Spanish democracy against a military coup in 1981. Had the American system included a non-partisan head of state with similar legitimacy, the constitutional crises of recent years might have unfolded very differently.

Unity in an Age of Fracture

America is experiencing a crisis of national identity. The symbols that once united Americans—the flag, the anthem, the Founding Fathers themselves—have become contested terrain in culture wars. Partisan media has created parallel realities in which Americans share neither facts nor values. Regional, racial, and ideological divisions have intensified to the point that scholars seriously discuss the possibility of national dissolution.

Into this fractured landscape, a constitutional monarchy would introduce something genuinely new: a living symbol of national unity who stands above and apart from political combat. Unlike the flag or the Constitution—inanimate objects that can be interpreted and contested—a monarch is a person who can speak, act, and embody national values in real time.

The psychological power of monarchy should not be underestimated. Human beings are evolved to understand hierarchy, to feel emotional connection to leaders, and to organize their social understanding around persons rather than abstractions. The genius of constitutional monarchy is that it channels these deep-seated tendencies toward a politically neutral figure, freeing the governmental process from the distortions of personality cult.

Consider how Americans already seek monarchical substitutes. The Kennedy family, the Bush and Clinton dynasties, even the treatment of figures like Oprah Winfrey or various celebrities—all reflect an unfulfilled longing for non-political figures of national significance. The celebrity worship that dominates American culture is, in part, a symptom of monarchical absence. Better to channel this human need toward an institution designed to serve the public good than to leave it to be exploited by entertainers, influencers, and demagogues.

The Separation of Dignity and Power

The core insight of constitutional monarchy is the separation of dignified and efficient functions of government. The monarch embodies the dignity, continuity, and symbolic authority of the state. The elected government exercises actual political power. This division has profound advantages.

First, it allows the head of government to be vigorously opposed without anyone feeling that opposition to the prime minister constitutes disloyalty to the nation itself. In America, criticizing the president often feels like—and is often characterized as—unpatriotic. The fusion of roles makes political opposition feel transgressive in a way it need not.

Second, it protects the symbolic functions of state from political contamination. State ceremonies, diplomatic receptions, the honoring of national heroes—all these occasions are diminished when presided over by a figure half the country views as a political enemy. A monarch can dignify these occasions in ways no politician can.

Third, it provides a career path for public-spirited individuals who have no taste for the combat of electoral politics. Many talented people who would make excellent servants of the nation are repelled by the modern campaign process. A royal household provides an alternative avenue for public service, attracting those whose gifts lie in diplomacy, ceremony, and representation rather than partisan warfare.

Addressing Objections

The objections to American monarchy are predictable but, upon examination, less compelling than they initially appear.

"Monarchy is undemocratic." This confuses democracy with republicanism. Democracy means rule by the people; it is a method of making collective decisions. Monarchy refers to a form of head of state. Constitutional monarchies like the United Kingdom, Canada, and Japan are fully democratic—their citizens vote, their parliaments legislate, their courts adjudicate. The monarch reigns but does not rule. Indeed, some scholars argue that constitutional monarchy better protects democracy by providing a neutral guardian of constitutional norms.

"Americans fought a revolution to reject monarchy." Americans fought a revolution to reject tyrannical government, taxation without representation, and denial of the rights of Englishmen. The Declaration of Independence's complaints against George III were complaints against his actions, not against the principle of monarchy itself. Many Founders admired the British constitutional system and sought to replicate its virtues. The rejection of monarchy was more contingent than principled—a consequence of the particular circumstances of 1776, not an eternal commitment.

"Hereditary succession is arbitrary and unfair." All systems for selecting leaders are arbitrary in some sense. Election rewards those skilled at campaigning—a skill set largely irrelevant to governing. Hereditary succession has the virtue of producing leaders trained from birth for their role, with no incentive to pander, no donors to reward, and no re-election to seek. Moreover, the arbitrariness of birth is precisely the point: it places someone in the highest symbolic office who cannot be accused of having schemed or fought their way there.

"Where would we find a royal family?" This is a practical question, not a principled objection. Various solutions present themselves. Descendants of historical American figures, a selection process followed by hereditary succession, or even inviting a junior line of an existing royal house are all possibilities. The initial selection would be a founding moment; thereafter, the hereditary principle would provide continuity.

"It would require a constitutional amendment." Indeed it would—a high bar that ensures such a change would only occur with broad national consensus. But the difficulty of the process is not an argument against the wisdom of the outcome. If Americans came to believe that constitutional monarchy would serve them better than the current system, the Constitution provides a mechanism for such a transformation.

A New Founding for a Divided Nation

The American experiment has achieved much, but it is now straining under contradictions the Founders did not foresee. The fusion of head of state and head of government in an age of media saturation and tribal politics has produced a presidency that divides rather than unites, that represents faction rather than nation.

Constitutional monarchy offers a proven alternative. The world's most stable, prosperous, and free societies are disproportionately constitutional monarchies. They have found a way to combine democratic governance with symbolic continuity, partisan politics with national unity, popular sovereignty with institutional stability.

America deserves a head of state who belongs to all Americans, who embodies the nation's continuity across generations, who stands above the partisan fray while protecting the constitutional order. America deserves a monarch—not an absolute ruler, but a constitutional sovereign who reigns over a free people.

The crown need not be a step backward. It might be the step forward that saves the republic from itself.

America needs a hereditary monarch.

I. The Separation of Symbol and Power Is Governance Wisdom, Not Contradiction

The American Founders made a philosophical error that has compounded for two and a half centuries: they conflated the symbolic head of state with the executive head of government. In doing so, they created a structural instability that no subsequent reform has adequately addressed.

Consider what a president must simultaneously be. The president is the commander-in-chief of the world's most powerful military. The president is the chief executive responsible for administering a federal bureaucracy of millions. The president is the chief diplomat. The president is the leader of a political party. And the president is the symbolic embodiment of American national identity — the figure who speaks at national tragedies, who lights the Christmas tree, who welcomes foreign dignitaries, who represents America's soul to the world.

These roles are not merely different. They are contradictory. When a partisan political figure — which every elected president necessarily is — also serves as the national symbol, the symbol becomes partisan. Half the country, at any given moment, despises the person who is supposed to represent them all. When Barack Obama spoke at Sandy Hook, millions of Americans who opposed his policies found themselves moved. When Donald Trump spoke at similar moments, millions of Americans who supported his policies found the symbolism contaminated by political opposition. The symbol cannot do its work when the symbol is also a combatant.

Constitutional monarchies solved this problem centuries ago. In the United Kingdom, the Prime Minister governs and leads the party that won election. The monarch reigns, embodying the nation across all political divides. When Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022, Britons of every political stripe — Conservative and Labour, Leave and Remain — mourned genuinely, because she had spent seventy years standing apart from their disputes. She had never been anyone's partisan. She could represent them all because she had never asked for any of their votes. Her authority derived not from defeating the other half of the country in an election but from being the country — or at least its living symbol.

The American political cycle has become pathological. Presidential campaigns now begin practically the day after an inauguration. The nations with the most stable, trusted political institutions in the developed world are disproportionately constitutional monarchies. The deepest American objection to monarchy is not practical but philosophical: the conviction, embedded in the Declaration of Independence, that all men are created equal and that just government derives from the consent of the governed. A hereditary monarch, the argument goes, violates the first principle by elevating one family above all others, and the second by removing the head of state from democratic accountability.

The question is not whether any differentiation of role and authority is compatible with equality, but whether a specific differentiation serves legitimate social functions. All governing authority — executive, military, diplomatic — would transfer entirely to an empowered Prime Minister accountable to Congress. The Sovereign would hold no veto, no policy authority, no command authority.

For the first sovereign, a constitutional convention would select from among distinguished American families — perhaps a family with multi-generational service, untainted by recent partisan controversy. Thereafter, succession would follow hereditary rules, with provisions for the Sovereign to be removed by supermajority of Congress in cases of severe unfitness.

The objection that no American family has sufficient prestige is empirically false. The Adams family, the Roosevelt family, the Eisenhower family — America has produced dynasties of service whose members command cross-partisan respect. The argument that Americans would never accept this underestimates the depth of exhaustion with the current system and the genuine human appetite for stable, uncontroversial institutional symbols.

America is a young country with an old problem: how to make a nation cohere across its enormous diversity of region, culture, religion, and politics. The current answer — elect a partisan leader and require everyone to treat them as a national symbol — has failed. The presidency has become a trophy of factional victory, its occupant beloved by supporters and reviled by opponents, its symbolic function destroyed by its political function.

A constitutional monarchy offers something that democratic elections structurally cannot: a head of state who belongs to everyone because they belong to no faction. The dignity of a crown that passes not by electoral victory but by dynastic succession is precisely its immunity from the divisions that elections necessarily create.

The American tradition of democratic self-governance need not be abandoned. It need only be refined — by learning from the world's most stable democracies that governing power and symbolic authority are better separated than combined, that some institutions serve the nation best precisely when they stand outside the contest for power.

The republic that the Founders built was extraordinary. But even extraordinary experiments can be improved by wisdom accumulated over centuries. Constitutional monarchy is not a step backward from democracy. In the nations that practice it, it is democracy's most stable form.

It is time to consider the crown.

  • Social Trust and Institutional Stability: Nations with hereditary heads of state consistently report higher levels of social trust, lower levels of political polarization, and stronger perceived legitimacy of governmental institutions.

The republic, in other words, has been given every advantage and has still underperformed.

Both are constitutional monarchies. Both are stable, prosperous, and democratic. No comparable republican system in a divided nation has demonstrated the same resilience.

One of the most powerful arguments for the American presidency is that it is earned — that any citizen can rise to the highest office through talent, effort, and the judgment of their fellow citizens. This is a beautiful ideal. It is also, in practice, a myth.

It does not require its citizens to believe the fiction that the most powerful person in the nation is simply the most talented. It locates the head of state in a family, assigns it ceremonial responsibilities, and — critically — limits its power.

The American presidency, by contrast, combines aristocratic reality with democratic pretense. This combination is more dangerous than either element alone. When citizens believe the presidency is meritocratic but observe that it is not, their disillusionment breeds cynicism. When they believe elections are free and fair but observe that money, media, and institutional gatekeeping determine the outcomes, their faith in democracy erodes.

A constitutional monarchy strips away these illusions. The monarch is there because of birth, not merit. No one pretends otherwise. And because no one pretends, there is no disillusionment. The real work of governance is left to elected politicians — prime ministers, chancellors, and parliaments — who are genuinely accountable, genuinely subject to electoral judgment, and genuinely answerable for policy outcomes.

A common objection to monarchy is that it is static — that a hereditary system enshrines the past and resists necessary change. This objection confuses the head of state with the government.

Policies are implemented by the prime minister and cabinet. Elections occur on regular schedules. If the populace desires change, it votes for change — and change happens.

What does not happen is the destabilizing drama of replacing the head of state. There is no succession crisis. There is no lame-duck period. There is no interregnum. The machinery of government continues to function even as political leadership rotates.

The American system, by contrast, produces enormous instability at every transition. Each election is an existential crisis. Each inauguration is a reset. Each new president attempts to undo the work of their predecessor. Executive orders are issued and revoked with metronomic regularity. The United States lurches from administration to administration, each one treating the previous eight years as a mistake to be corrected. This is not governance; it is pendulum warfare.

V. The Symbolic Power of Permanence

There is a deeper, more philosophical point here about the human relationship with symbols and continuity.

Nations are not merely administrative units. They are communities of memory, meaning, and shared identity. Every functioning civilization has developed institutions that embody permanence — cathedrals, constitutions, traditions, ceremonies. These institutions serve a psychological and social function: they connect the present to the past, the individual to the collective, and the ephemeral to the enduring.

A hereditary monarchy is, in the context of the state, such an institution. It is a living symbol of national continuity. When the British monarch opens Parliament, when the Japanese Emperor presides over ceremonies of renewal, when the King of Norway addresses his people — these are not merely quaint traditions. They are rituals that reinforce social cohesion by reminding citizens that they are part of something larger than any single election, any single politician, or any single generation.

The American republic has no such institution. The presidency tries to fill this role, but fails precisely because it is contested. You cannot have a symbol of unity that 40% of the population voted against. You cannot have a ritual of continuity when the ritual is redesigned every four to eight years. The American attempt to make the president both head of state and head of government is, in symbolic terms, a structural impossibility.

This is not a trivial concern. Social science research consistently demonstrates that nations with strong symbolic institutions experience higher levels of social trust, civic engagement, and national cohesion. The monarchy is not merely decorative; it is functional in the deepest sense. It provides a container for national identity that is not subject to the fragmentation of partisan politics.

"But monarchy is undemocratic."

This objection assumes that the head of state must be elected to be democratic. But in a constitutional monarchy, all actual power resides in elected institutions. The monarch reigns but does not rule. The people govern themselves through their elected representatives. What they surrender is not democratic power but the fiction that the head of state represents their personal choice.

Moreover, democracy is not a single institutional arrangement. It is a principle — the principle that legitimate governance requires the consent of the governed. That consent is expressed through elections for the legislature and executive, through free press, through independent courts, and through robust civil liberties. A hereditary monarch who possesses no governing power and operates under constitutional constraint does not violate this principle any more than an elected president who also possesses no governing power (as in Germany, where the president is largely ceremonial).

"But what if the monarch is terrible?"

A constitutional monarchy provides for this contingency. In nations like the United Kingdom and Spain, the monarch's role is defined by constitution and convention. Abolition of the monarchy requires only an act of parliament — not a revolution, not a coup. The people retain ultimate sovereignty. What they gain is a head of state who is predictable rather than arbitrary, permanent rather than temporary, and unifying rather than divisive.

"But America has no tradition of monarchy."

This is true, and it is perhaps the strongest practical objection. But traditions are not immutable. They are created, maintained, and changed by the choices of living people. The American founders themselves debated this question extensively. Alexander Hamilton, at the Constitutional Convention, proposed a president who would serve "during good behaviour" — essentially, for life. He was overruled, but his argument — that a permanent executive would be more stable and less susceptible to demagoguery — has only grown more persuasive with time.

Furthermore, America does have a tradition of symbolic continuity. The rituals of the presidency — the oath of office, the State of the Union, the national ceremonies — all attempt to fill the role of a unifying symbolic institution. They fail because the officeholder is partisan. A hereditary monarch would make these rituals authentic rather than performative.

VII. What Would It Look Like?

The proposal need not be radical. Consider a model:

  1. A hereditary monarch serves as head of state with strictly ceremonial powers: receiving ambassadors, opening Parliament, bestowing honors, and serving as a symbolic representative of national unity.
  2. A prime minister, elected by the Congress (or by the people directly), serves as head of government with full executive authority.
  3. The monarch's powers are defined by constitutional statute and can be modified or abolished by a supermajority of Congress and a national referendum.
  4. The monarch is bound by strict non-partisanship and may not comment on, endorse, or interfere with any political matter.

This model — essentially the constitutional monarchy of the Netherlands or Denmark, adapted for American scale and culture — preserves democratic self-governance while adding a layer of symbolic stability and unifying continuity that the elected presidency cannot provide.

Conclusion

The American republic was a bold experiment, and for much of its history, a successful one. But experiments that fail to adapt eventually become dogmas. The evidence — both philosophical and empirical — suggests that the hereditary constitutional monarchy is a superior institutional arrangement for a head of state. It provides unity without partisanship, continuity without stagnation, symbolism without fiction, and stability without the concentration of power.

The question is not whether we love our republic. The question is whether we love our republic so much that we are willing to sacrifice our country's well-being on its altar. The constitutional monarchies of the world are not relics of a feudal past. They are modern, democratic, prosperous, and free. They are, in many measurable respects, more democratic, more prosperous, and more free than the republics that occupy the same tier of development.

America does not need a tyrant. It does not need an autocrat. What it needs is a symbol — permanent, dignified, above the fray — around which a fractured nation can begin to heal. The crown, worn lightly and constrained constitutionally, offers precisely that. It is time to consider whether the experiment of the elected presidency has run its course, and whether a different arrangement might better serve the nation the founders sought to build.
